questions.stem: Scenario: Lowell Freight's invoice job takes every vendor invoice through the same five steps in the same order: read the PDF, match the order, check the amount, flag exceptions and post. A developer proposes an agent that picks its own steps, because agents are flexible. Which two statements does the page support? (Select two.)

options.text: An agent suits it, since flexibility is worth its price on every job
options.says: Ruled out because "Only then does autonomy earn its price", and the path here needs no model to decide what to do next.

options.text: Code that fixes the sequence is cheaper, testable and auditable
options.says: The path is known, so the code should run it: "If you can write the steps down and their order, the code should run them, because deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable and auditable" (module 79, page 1). The workflow rung is chosen when "The path is known in advance and the steps differ in kind".

options.text: A single call with a long prompt suits it, since the sequence is a detail
options.says: Ruled out because a single call suits "one transformation with the input in hand", and five steps in an order are more than that.

options.text: A team of agents suits it, with one worker answering for each stage
options.says: Ruled out because the team rung needs "the volume of reading exceeds one context", and the steps here run one after another.

options.text: A workflow suits it, since the path is known in advance
options.says: The path is known, so the code should run it: "If you can write the steps down and their order, the code should run them, because deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable and auditable" (module 79, page 1). The workflow rung is chosen when "The path is known in advance and the steps differ in kind".

origin.section: The ladder of patterns

questions.stem: Scenario: Ostrander Bank wants to serve small business owners by chat, a group it has never been able to staff. The sponsor accepts that early answers will be less accurate and asks that adoption be tracked. Which value pillar does the sponsor want served?

options.text: Transformation, since it opens up something that could not be done before
options.says: The pillar "Accepts a lower first-pass accuracy and a pilot, and measures adoption", which is what the sponsor asked for (module 79, page 1).

options.text: Efficiency, since the same work needs less effort for each unit that is handled
options.says: Ruled out because efficiency claims "The same work, with less effort per unit", and there was no work done for this group before.

options.text: Productivity, since the bank's own staff get more done in each working week
options.says: Ruled out because productivity means "People get more done", and no staff member is the beneficiary here.

options.text: Cost, since the work in total is priced lower than the bank pays today
options.says: Ruled out because the cost pillar claims "Work costs less in total", and the sponsor named a new service.

origin.section: The five value pillars

questions.stem: Scenario: Brindle Law's drafting task is worth about forty chats, and four agents would each need the whole case file and the other agents' drafts at every step. A designer proposes a coordinator with four subagents. What does the page conclude?

options.text: Use the team of four subagents as the designer proposes
options.says: Ruled out because value is only the third condition: "it needs independence, volume and value together".

options.text: Use the team, with a larger window for each subagent
options.says: Ruled out because the first test fails whatever the window size: "A team that fails the first test is a worse single agent".

options.text: Use a workflow with four fixed calls in a set order
options.says: Ruled out because a workflow is for a known path: "Is the path known? Then it is a workflow, and it costs one chat per step", and drafting that depends on other drafts has no fixed order.

options.text: Use one worker that holds all of the material itself
options.says: A team needs independent parts, and these share one context: "cannot be split without losing information" (module 80, page 1).

origin.section: When a team earns its cost

questions.stem: Scenario: Fable Retail's reviewer rates three designs. Design A is rejected and costs 30,000 a month. Design B needs a revision and costs 50,000. Design C is approved and costs 70,000. Which does the cheapest-adequate rule pick?

options.text: A, because the cheapest design wins whatever its verdict happens to be
options.says: Ruled out because "a cheaper design with a missing feedback loop is not cheaper, only unfinished".

options.text: B, since price decides only among those that were not turned down
options.says: Price comes last and among the survivors: "Price enters last, and only among the designs that were not rejected" (module 80, page 2).

options.text: C, because only an approved design may be chosen for a launch
options.says: Ruled out because the rule picks "the cheapest of those", and a design that needs revision is not a rejected one.

options.text: None of them, because a design must be approved before it can be priced
options.says: Ruled out because "when every design is rejected there is no winner", and here two designs survive.

origin.section: An architecture review as a rubric

questions.stem: Scenario: A coordinator at Marlow Analytics sends four subagents to read hundreds of pages each, and its window is full before it writes the report. The subagents must still run in parallel. Which contract change fixes the design?

options.text: Each subagent reads only the first source
options.says: Ruled out because the page asks for the objective and boundaries so "that two subagents do not research the same thing or leave a gap between them".

options.text: Each subagent forwards the pages it read, trimmed to fit
options.says: Ruled out because the transcript is the problem and not its size: "The subagent's reading is thrown away when it finishes".

options.text: Each subagent waits for the coordinator to ask, so nothing arrives unplanned
options.says: Ruled out because "What goes back is the finding, with its source, in the contract's shape".

options.text: Each worker hands back its conclusion with a citation, in a fixed shape
options.says: A subagent's reading is thrown away when it finishes, so what goes back is a digest in the contract's shape: "Return a digest, not a transcript" (module 80, page 2). The finding with its source leaves the coordinator's window free for writing.

origin.section: What a subagent gets, and what it returns

questions.stem: Scenario: Kite Pay's payment tool honours an idempotency key, but the agent builds that key from the current time on each attempt, so a retry after a lost response pays twice. Which change fixes the design?

options.text: Make a fresh value for each attempt and log every one of them
options.says: Ruled out because "The key is made once, before the first call, from what identifies the task (the order and the action), and it is stored with the task".

options.text: Derive the label once from the order and the action, and reuse it for every repeat
options.says: The key must name the intention and be made once, before the first call, from what identifies the task (module 81, page 1). The page says "A new key for each attempt turns the retry into a new refund", which is the flaw here.

options.text: Lengthen the key, to keep two different payments from sharing one
options.says: Ruled out because the flaw is that the value changes between attempts, and "The key names the intention, not the attempt".

options.text: Save the key before the call and the payment after it, in two steps
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "Record the key together with the effect", in one transaction.

origin.section: A retry is safe only when the repeat is recognised

questions.stem: Scenario: A runner at Oaken Labs treats every tool error alike, with five attempts and growing pauses, and a call refused for lack of permission uses all five. Which rule belongs in its design?

options.text: Give every attempt a fresh idempotency key, so the tool sees each as new
options.says: Ruled out because "The key names the intention, not the attempt", and a missing permission is not a problem of recognising repeats.

options.text: Open the breaker for the agent and have every later task skip the tool
options.says: Ruled out because the breaker counts "consecutive failures for one agent", and a missing permission is a fact about the account.

options.text: Classify faults: repeat passing ones up to a cap, fail permanent ones at once
options.says: A refusal is a fatal failure, and the runner "never retries the second" kind (module 81, page 1). A timeout or a rate limit is transient and is repeated up to a fixed number of calls.

options.text: Raise the attempts to ten with longer pauses to outlast the fault
options.says: Ruled out because "An unlimited retry is a way to spend money while nothing changes", and ten is the same mistake.

origin.section: Retries have limits, and not every failure is a retry

questions.stem: Scenario: A breaker around Quarry Labs' search agent opens during an outage. After its cooldown one probe call goes through and fails. Which behaviour keeps spending low for the rest of the outage?

options.text: It reverts to refusing requests at once until a further pause has passed
options.says: A failed probe opens the breaker again: "A success closes it; a failure opens it again" (module 81, page 1). The agent is not reached until the next probe, which saves calls in a long outage.

options.text: It resets its count of failures and allows the next three calls
options.says: Ruled out because "A success resets the count, so scattered failures do not open it", which concerns the closed state.

options.text: It closes and lets all traffic back through again
options.says: Ruled out because only a success closes the breaker, and the open state is the one in which "Calls are refused at once, without reaching the agent".

options.text: It stays half-open and lets further probes through one after another
options.says: Ruled out because "One probe call goes through", and a failure sends the breaker back to open.

origin.section: A circuit breaker stops the spending

questions.stem: Scenario: Larch Mutual's claims assistant answers policy questions for staff from documents that change often, and the way through a request never varies. A designer proposes agents. Which two statements does the capstone support? (Select two.)

options.text: One agent holding every tool suits it and is simpler to audit
options.says: Ruled out because autonomous agents come with "higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors".

options.text: A coordinated crew would cost about 15 times a chat, and the value does not pay it
options.says: The capstone sets the rung: "an augmented call with a small fixed workflow, not an agent, because the path is known", and it notes "A team of agents would cost about 15 times a chat, and the value does not pay it" (module 93, page 1).

options.text: One plain call with all the policy text pasted in suits it and keeps the route simple
options.says: Ruled out because the design needs "The index is replaced when a document changes", and pasted text goes stale.

options.text: A team of agents suits it and handles many documents that change often
options.says: Ruled out because the ladder reaches a team only when "it becomes a team only when the parts are independent and the value pays for the team", and reading many documents that change often is not that.

options.text: A small fixed workflow around a retrieval-backed call suits the known path
options.says: The capstone sets the rung: "an augmented call with a small fixed workflow, not an agent, because the path is known", and it notes "A team of agents would cost about 15 times a chat, and the value does not pay it" (module 93, page 1).

origin.section: One design, seven decisions

questions.stem: Scenario: A claims question at Larch Mutual shares no word with any document that the reader may read, though it does match a contract that only the partnership team may read. What does the chain return?

options.text: The contract chunk, marked as restricted to the partnership
options.says: Ruled out because "Documents the reader may not read are removed first, then the rest are ranked".

options.text: A hold for lack of evidence, with no answer given
options.says: The chain removes first and ranks after: "a question that shares nothing with any readable document gets no evidence" (module 93, page 1).

options.text: The best readable chunk, even though it shares no word
options.says: Ruled out because "the rest are ranked by the words they share with the question", so a document that shares no word is never ranked and no chunk is returned.

options.text: An answer from the model alone, flagged as unsupported
options.says: Ruled out because "an answer whose quote is missing is held as unsupported", and the chain never sends it out with a flag.

origin.section: The chain, request by request

questions.stem: Scenario: A review at Larch Mutual of a proposal finds no way back to the previous model if the new one fails, and no other flaw. What does the written review record and conclude?

options.text: A medium item in P4, so it goes back for revision
options.says: Ruled out because a medium flaw "weakens a design without breaking it", and a missing way back is a flaw that can cause harm that cannot be undone.

options.text: A low item in P6, so it is approved with a note
options.says: Ruled out because the low bullet reads "It is recorded and does not hold the design back", and a missing rollback is not low.

options.text: A high-severity item in P1, so it goes back for revision
options.says: Ruled out because "reject if any finding is high", so a high finding is not a revision.

options.text: A high-severity item in P4, so the design is rejected
options.says: A high finding rejects: "The design is rejected until it is fixed" (module 93, page 2).

origin.section: A finding has three parts

questions.stem: Scenario: Nettle Support edits the description of one tool every Friday to tune its wording, and the cache hit rate falls after each edit even though the system prompt and the messages never change. What explains it?

options.text: The cache lifetime ends on Fridays, so entries expire together and are rebuilt
options.says: Ruled out because the page gives the cause as an edit inside the prefix: "The edit is inside the prefix, so everything from there on is a new entry".

options.text: Tool descriptions count as dynamic text, so they sit after the breakpoint and are never cached
options.says: Ruled out because the documentation fixes the order of the whole request "as tools, then system, then messages", so tools lie in front of the breakpoint.

options.text: Definitions lead the request, so altering one invalidates everything that is after it
options.says: The documented order is tools, system, messages: "a change to a tool definition invalidates the system prompt and the messages that follow it" (module 82, page 1).

options.text: The system prompt is hashed together with the date, so a weekly edit always changes it
options.says: Ruled out because the page names the tool edit as the cause, and says the tool list should be treated "as a stable asset".

origin.section: Why the order matters: the cached prefix

questions.stem: Scenario: Two workloads at Cobble Insurance both mark a breakpoint after their third block. Their first two blocks are identical, and their third blocks differ by one sentence. How much of the prefix can they share?

options.text: The first two blocks, since those are identical in both prompts
options.says: Ruled out because "If any block differs, or either prompt has no breakpoint, nothing is reusable".

options.text: Nothing, since the match must hold for each piece up to the cut-off
options.says: Reuse is all or nothing: "nothing is reusable and the answer is zero" (module 82, page 2).

options.text: Most of it, since only one sentence differs between the two prompts
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "If any block differs, or either prompt has no breakpoint, nothing is reusable", however small the difference.

options.text: All of it, provided that both prompts name the same model
options.says: Ruled out because the check is on the blocks: "every block up to it must match in name and text".

origin.section: When two requests can share a prefix

questions.stem: Scenario: Hollin Labs upgrades its assistant to a newer release and copies across a prompt sentence that fixed an over-eager habit on the older one. Nobody has tested the sentence on the release. Which two steps does the page support? (Select two.)

options.text: Keep the line and trust that models in one family behave alike
options.says: Ruled out because "Copy the prompt that worked on the current model; models in one family behave alike" is the page's rejected trap.

options.text: Treat the technique as measured on the old model until re-checked against your own evals
options.says: The guide says "where a technique names a specific model, treat it as measured on that model and re-check it against your own evals before applying it to another", so the design runs an evaluation set on every candidate model and prompt change (module 82, page 2).

options.text: Keep the line and add a second one that repeats it in stronger words
options.says: Ruled out because "a technique is measured on a model, so it is re-checked against your own evaluation before it is applied to another".

options.text: Drop every line that fixed a habit and trust that new models need none
options.says: Ruled out because "an instruction that fixed a behaviour on one model can be unnecessary or harmful on another", so it is tested, not dropped by default.

options.text: Run the evaluation set on the new model and see whether the results back the line
options.says: The guide says "where a technique names a specific model, treat it as measured on that model and re-check it against your own evals before applying it to another", so the design runs an evaluation set on every candidate model and prompt change (module 82, page 2).

origin.section: Choosing a model and shaping the context

questions.stem: Scenario: Pallet Support's smaller model costs half as much per token as its larger one, but it needs about three attempts for each ticket, while the larger one answers once. Which comparison does the page require?

options.text: The full bill for one completed item, tries included
options.says: The comparison is per task: "a weaker model that needs three attempts or a longer prompt can cost more than a stronger one that answers once" (module 82, page 2).

options.text: The price of a token for each of the two models
options.says: Ruled out because "the cheapest model per token is not always the cheapest per task".

options.text: The latency of one attempt on each model
options.says: Ruled out because latency is a limit that rules models out and "Price comes last because it is the only fact that cannot make a model wrong".

options.text: The size of the context window of each model
options.says: Ruled out because the page gives no such link, and the tier is "found by evaluating the task, not by reading a model's name".

origin.section: A model is chosen for a workload

questions.stem: Scenario: Isle Travel's legacy caller times out after 2,000 ms. The assistant's slow case, the 95th percentile, is 1,500 ms, and the team adds a safety margin of 600 ms. How should the gateway deliver the answer?

options.text: Synchronously, since the median call fits well inside the limit
options.says: Ruled out because a median hides the slow case: "The example's twelve timings have a mean of 1,441 ms, a median of 980 ms and a 95th percentile of 4,800 ms".

options.text: By raising the caller's timeout, since that changes nothing in the gateway
options.says: Ruled out because "Raising the legacy system's timeout is often not possible and moves the problem into a system nobody owns".

options.text: By accept-and-poll, since the tail figure with its buffer is over the caller's limit
options.says: The gateway "compares the slow case (the 95th-percentile time plus a safety margin) with the caller's timeout" (module 84, page 2); 2,100 ms is over 2,000 ms.

options.text: By accept-and-poll only if the caller asks for the result to be delayed, which it rarely does
options.says: Ruled out because the choice is the gateway's: "If it does not, the gateway uses accept-and-poll".

origin.section: Four decisions in code

questions.stem: Scenario: A new project is onboarded to Larch Telecom's gateway with a budget of zero because finance has not yet set one. Its first request arrives with a small estimate. What does admission return?

options.text: Allow, since the estimate is small and the spend so far is zero
options.says: Ruled out because admission is decided against the budget: "A request that would bring the spend to more than the budget blocks".

options.text: Warn, since a first request always warns whatever the budget may be
options.says: Ruled out because a warning belongs to the case "Reaching 80 percent warns", and a zero budget is blocked before that.

options.text: Block, since a ceiling that is not positive leaves no room
options.says: The edge is exact: "A budget that is not positive blocks" (module 84, page 2).

options.text: Allow once, then block when the spend reaches eighty percent of nothing
options.says: Ruled out because the rule has no free first request, and eighty percent is a point of warning and not of blocking: "Reaching 80 percent warns, and exactly 80 percent warns".

origin.section: Four decisions in code

questions.stem: Scenario: A team at Marsh Retail is close to its budget, and the policy names no cheaper model for the model it uses for refund drafting. The team is not blocked. What does the gateway do with its next request?

options.text: Keeps its original pick
options.says: Degrading needs a named entry: "when it has no cheaper entry the model is kept" (module 84, page 2).

options.text: Switches to the cheapest model in the whole table
options.says: Ruled out because the replacement is "a cheaper one that the policy names", not a free choice of the cheapest.

options.text: Blocks the request until the budget has been raised by the platform team
options.says: Ruled out because "A blocked team gets no model", and the team here is near its budget and not blocked: "a team is warned, then degraded, then stopped, in that order".

options.text: Switches to a model of the same tier from another vendor, to stay within the budget
options.says: Ruled out because the route table is the gateway's: "Route each task to a model by one table".

origin.section: Four decisions in code

questions.stem: Scenario: Tern Fuel's usage report has a row for a model that the price table does not list. The report job must still finish. What should showback do with that row?

options.text: Price it at the average of the listed models
options.says: Ruled out because showback is computed "at the price of the row's model", and an average of other models is not that price.

options.text: Skip the row and carry on with the rest of the report
options.says: Ruled out because "Each team sees what it spent", and a skipped row would hide spend from the team that incurred it.

options.text: Price it at zero and add a note to the report
options.says: Ruled out because "Every token kind has its own price", and a price of zero makes the usage free in the report.

options.text: Reject that line, naming the one with no rate
options.says: A gateway does not guess: "A row whose model has no price is refused, because a gateway never guesses a price" (module 84, page 2).

origin.section: Four decisions in code

questions.stem: Scenario: Quay Retail's assistant must give each branch's refund total for February. The figures sit in a table, and the team has cut the table into text chunks, after which the model adds the numbers by eye and gets them wrong. Which two statements does the page support? (Select two.)

options.text: A longer chunk size brings every branch's rows together and fixes the sums
options.says: Ruled out because "the cut follows the structure of the data" and not a length, and longer chunks would still leave the model adding numbers by eye.

options.text: An embedding index over the rows matches each figure by meaning and gives the totals
options.says: Ruled out because embedding models "can miss crucial exact matches", and add nothing up.

options.text: Slicing the rows into fragments leaves the sums to guesswork
options.says: When the answer lives in a table or a database the mechanism is a structured query run by a tool, which is "Exact, and able to total or filter", while cutting the table "adds numbers by eye" is the failure it avoids (module 85, page 1).

options.text: A keyword index on the word refund finds every row and gives the totals
options.says: Ruled out because a keyword index "matches the exact string", and it does not total or filter.

options.text: A database query issued through a tool sums and filters exactly
options.says: When the answer lives in a table or a database the mechanism is a structured query run by a tool, which is "Exact, and able to total or filter", while cutting the table "adds numbers by eye" is the failure it avoids (module 85, page 1).

origin.section: Match the mechanism to the data and the question

questions.stem: Scenario: Fallow Utilities' retrieval returns a chunk that reads only "The charge is waived for the first month", and users cannot tell which plan it belongs to. Which repair does the page support?

options.text: Return twenty chunks for every question, to make the plan's name turn up in one
options.says: Ruled out because "Returning more chunks per question does not help either".

options.text: Cut the text into smaller windows and let each chunk hold fewer unrelated words
options.says: Ruled out because "A smaller window cuts in more places and separates more sentences from their neighbours".

options.text: Ask the model to guess the plan from the rest of the conversation when it answers
options.says: Ruled out because "Retrieval hands the model a chunk without its document", and a guess gives no evidence to cite.

options.text: Put the document title and section name in front of each piece before indexing
options.says: Structure supplies the context a chunk lacks: "The pipeline already knows the document title and the section name" (module 85, page 1).

origin.section: A chunk has to stand alone

questions.stem: Scenario: Tarn Dental's entire knowledge base is about 60,000 tokens, edited a few times a year, and the team plans a vector database with chunking and reranking. What does the page advise first?

options.text: Build the vector database
options.says: Ruled out because "A pipeline adds stages that each can fail", and a corpus this small needs none of them.

options.text: Put the complete corpus into a cached prompt
options.says: A corpus under about 200,000 tokens needs no index: "No stage can fail and nothing can be missed" (module 85, page 1).

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the corpus
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "The Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning", and weights are weak when facts change and a source must be shown.

options.text: Split the corpus across several agents, each of which holds a part of it
options.says: Ruled out because the corpus fits one window, and a team of agents is justified only when "the reading that has to be done is larger than one agent can hold".

origin.section: Match the mechanism to the data and the question

questions.stem: Scenario: Dunmore Legal switches its retrieval from one embedding model to a newer one. It embeds only the documents that change from now on, and keeps the old embeddings for the rest. Recall on its labelled questions falls at once. What explains it?

options.text: The newer model needs a larger chunk size, so the old chunks are now too small
options.says: Ruled out because "Size then follows from the unit", the structure of the data, and not from the embedding model that scores the chunks.

options.text: The old vectors are stale copies of their documents, so a re-index would clear them
options.says: Ruled out because "An index is stale when a chunk no longer matches its source", and these old vectors still match their documents.

options.text: Vectors from two different encoders do not share one space, so the whole index must be rebuilt
options.says: The page gives the rule: "Vectors made by two models are not in one space, so the index must be rebuilt as a whole" (module 85, page 2).

options.text: The keyword index must be rebuilt first, then the vectors
options.says: Ruled out because the keyword index does not depend on the embeddings, and the recall falls because "queries embedded by the new model will be compared with chunks embedded by the old one".

origin.section: What a re-index must do

questions.stem: Scenario: Ferris Systems' staff each paste the company's access string for the model supplier into their own scripts, and a former employee still has a working copy. The security lead asks for a design that limits the damage of a leaked or abandoned copy. What fits?

options.text: A proxy that holds the master secret itself and issues every person a separate token
options.says: The documentation lists the gain of a gateway: "the provider key stays server-side; developers hold gateway credentials instead" (module 86, page 1), so offboarding revokes one credential.

options.text: A rotation of the shared access string every quarter, announced by e-mail
options.says: Ruled out because the string stays in every pair of hands between rotations, whereas with a gateway "a leaked developer credential is not a leaked provider key".

options.text: A prompt rule that tells the agent never to reveal the string it was given
options.says: Ruled out because "a line in the system prompt is a request to the model and not a control".

options.text: A separate supplier account for each team, with one shared string inside each of those accounts
options.says: Ruled out because a shared string in each team keeps the same leak, and the page puts the provider credential in one place, "which all the forwarded traffic uses".

origin.section: A gateway: one place for credentials, limits and records

questions.stem: Scenario: Mallow Cloud's MCP server requests every permission up front when a person connects, so that nobody sees a second consent prompt. A reviewer objects. What does the guidance say instead?

options.text: Begin with read access and widen it when a privileged operation is first attempted
options.says: The guidance is progressive: "Implement a progressive, least-privilege scope model", starting from read operations (module 86, page 1).

options.text: Ask for every scope the server offers, once at the start
options.says: Ruled out because "A token with every scope granted up front makes a stolen token worth the whole system".

options.text: Ask for one broad scope that covers all operations, and log each use of it afterwards
options.says: Ruled out because "Poor scope design increases token compromise impact, elevates user friction, and obscures audit trails".

options.text: Pass the user's own token on to the downstream service, so no scope is needed
options.says: Ruled out because "Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden in the authorization specification".

origin.section: Whose rights a call uses

questions.stem: Scenario: Pewter Labs merges its 40 tools into 8 tools, each with a switch argument, hoping to cure wrong tool selection. Selection does not improve. Which two statements explain it? (Select two.)

options.text: A switch argument is rejected by the platform as an unsupported parameter
options.says: Ruled out because the merge is rejected for a different reason: "Merging tools into one with a mode argument is not a cure".

options.text: Eight tools are still more than a request can hold, so the list must shrink
options.says: Ruled out because the page puts trouble where Claude's ability to pick the right tool "degrades once you exceed" the thirty to fifty mark, and eight is far below it.

options.text: The choice among behaviours is hidden from the model's own judgement
options.says: Merging "hides the behaviours from the model's own choice and leaves the number of capabilities the same" (module 86, page 2), so nothing was removed and the choice is only moved into an argument.

options.text: Merged tools lose their descriptions, so selection has no information left
options.says: Ruled out because "the descriptions are what the model chooses by", and a merge keeps them.

options.text: The number of capabilities is the same as before the change
options.says: Merging "hides the behaviours from the model's own choice and leaves the number of capabilities the same" (module 86, page 2), so nothing was removed and the choice is only moved into an argument.

origin.section: Three costs of too many capabilities

questions.stem: Scenario: An audit of Quill Support's agent lists a tool that the role needs and the agent holds, and the logs show no use of it in twelve months. What does the audit do with it?

options.text: Removes it, since a tool that is never used is only an attack surface

options.text: A requirement is complete once it carries a figure, a method of measuring it and a named owner
options.says: The page says "A requirement is complete when it has a number, a way to measure it and a person who owns it; a requirement missing one of the three goes back to the stakeholder as a question" (module 91, page 1).

options.text: A requirement is complete when it names the model that will meet it
options.says: Ruled out because the heading reads "Discovery ends in numbers and an owner".

options.text: A requirement is complete when the sponsor has signed it and engineers have read it once
options.says: Ruled out because "Fast", "accurate" and "safe" are not answers, "because nobody can fail them".

origin.section: Discovery ends in numbers and an owner

questions.stem: Scenario: In the options table of a design record, the entry for the costliest design carries a two-word rationale, "Too much". A reviewer asks for a change. What should that entry say instead?

options.text: A single word that names the main cost of the option
options.says: Ruled out because "the most expensive option and the slowest to answer" is a reason that "can be argued with", and one word cannot be.

options.text: A reference to the sponsor's budget for the year
options.says: Ruled out because "An option that misses a service level is not a candidate, however cheap", and the reason is a checkable fact about the option, not a budget name.

options.text: A sentence with a checkable reason, such as top price and slow reply
options.says: The page asks for argument: "A rejected option has a reason in a sentence" (module 91, page 1).

options.text: The name of the engineer who first rejected the option, for traceability
options.says: Ruled out because the reader's question is "why not the simple thing", and a name does not answer it.

origin.section: Options, and the rule for the recommendation

questions.stem: Scenario: The one-page note that Vane Rail's architect wrote for the funder describes the saving in detail and says nothing of what the proposal gives up. A colleague objects. What should the note also contain?

options.text: The price paid, the exposure that remains and the decision requested
options.says: The summary follows an order: "what improves, what it costs, what is at risk and what is asked" (module 91, page 1).

options.text: The break-even derivation, to let the funder check the arithmetic
options.says: Ruled out because the derivation belongs to the engineer's layer, and "The summary is first because the sponsor stops reading early".

options.text: The list of model settings, to let the funder confirm the build
options.says: Ruled out because the sponsor decides and the engineer builds, and settings are "the numbers that produced it" for the engineer.

options.text: A second saving figure for a more optimistic case, to balance the first
options.says: Ruled out because "Leaving out the downside is the common failure", and a second saving adds to the upside only.

origin.section: The trade-off, told

questions.stem: Scenario: A service level promises availability of at least 99.5 percent, written as 995 per mille. The month's measurement is 990 per mille. How does the report read?

options.text: Short of the floor by 5, counted in the unit of the target
options.says: A miss is reported with its size: "A miss says by how much" (module 91, page 2).

options.text: Failed, with the size of the gap left unstated in the report
options.says: Ruled out because a bare failure "starts an argument that a number would have ended".

options.text: Met, with the measurement inside a rounding margin
options.says: Ruled out because "A ceiling is met at or below it and a floor is met at or above it", and 990 is below the floor.

options.text: Short by 5 percent of the monthly availability target
options.says: Ruled out because the unit is the target's own: "The target has a number and a unit and a direction".

origin.section: The example

questions.stem: Scenario: Two months into a pilot, Dray Finance's team sees that its accuracy target for the costly segment will not be met by the agreed deadline. How should it handle the promise?

options.text: Keep quiet about the shortfall until the date
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "Say early what the design cannot promise".

options.text: Amend it through the channel that made it, with a reason, before the due day
options.says: The page gives the habit: "change a promise through the same channel that made it, with a reason, before the date it matters" (module 91, page 2).

options.text: Report the overall average instead of the segment
options.says: Ruled out because "Promise what you measure and measure what you promise", and the average hides the costly segment.

options.text: Move the target in the next sprint plan, without telling the sponsor or the review board
options.says: Ruled out because the sponsor's own channel is "A regular review of the segments, the saving and the open risks, with the decisions it needs", and a target moved in a sprint plan never reaches it.

origin.section: Aligning expectations

questions.stem: Scenario: Larch Mutual's architect has a finished review: a conclusion, a count per domain and twenty-two itemised flaws, and must present it to the sponsor and the engineers. How should the document be arranged?

options.text: The flaws first in domain order, then the conclusion and the count at the end
options.says: Ruled out because "A list ordered only by domain buries the high findings in the middle", and the sponsor stops early.

options.text: The count first, then a narrative of the design, then the flaws with no conclusion
options.says: Ruled out because a review without a conclusion leaves the sponsor nothing to decide: "The sponsor stops at the verdict and the scorecard".

options.text: The engineers' evidence first, to let the sponsor read the analysis before the conclusion
options.says: Ruled out because "the engineers read the findings", and the sponsor does not read the analysis.

options.text: Lead with the headline outcome, follow with a tally by area, then the ranked details
options.says: The review is written for two readers: "the verdict first, then the scorecard, then the findings in their order, each with the evidence from the design and the fix" (module 93, page 2).

origin.section: Writing the review

questions.stem: Scenario: Eland Systems fetches its policy from the admin console, and the security lead decides that no developer may begin without the current policy, even when the network is down and work stops. Which setting expresses that decision?

options.text: availableModels, which restricts the models a developer may pick
options.says: Ruled out because it is a list of models: "The lock is `availableModels`, a list".

options.text: disableSideloadFlags, which rejects the options that load a plugin
options.says: Ruled out because that key rejects the flags "that sideload plugins, agents and MCP servers", and has nothing to do with fetching.

options.text: forceRemoteSettingsRefresh, which makes startup fail closed
options.says: The default is to carry on: "If the fetch fails, Claude Code continues on the last policy it cached, or on none, and warns, unless `forceRemoteSettingsRefresh` is set, which makes startup fail closed" (module 92, page 1).

options.text: allowManagedHooksOnly, which stops every unmanaged hook from running
options.says: Ruled out because that key means "only managed hooks run", and says nothing of a start without the policy.

origin.section: Server-managed settings and their limits

questions.stem: Scenario: A platform team caps effort at high in managed settings. A project file sets medium and a user file sets max. Which two statements does the page support? (Select two.)

options.text: The project file's cap is ignored and only managed settings may set one
options.says: Ruled out because the cap is one of the few "security exceptions in which a stricter lower value counts", so the project file's value is weighed and not ignored.

options.text: The most restrictive setting wins, so the lowest of the three values is in force
options.says: The page gives the rule: "when several levels set a cap, the lowest applies, so a developer may lower the organisation's cap and nobody can raise it" (module 92, page 1).

options.text: Max is in force and the user file is read last
options.says: Ruled out because "a cap of `xhigh` or `max` in the managed file would be no cap at all for the levels it was meant to hold back".

options.text: High is in force and managed settings outrank every other level for this key
options.says: Ruled out because the key is one of the two that go the other way, where "a stricter value is always welcome".

options.text: Nobody can loosen the organisation's ceiling, though a developer may tighten it
options.says: The page gives the rule: "when several levels set a cap, the lowest applies, so a developer may lower the organisation's cap and nobody can raise it" (module 92, page 1).

origin.section: Locks you build from lists, and security exceptions

questions.stem: Scenario: A developer at Gorse Bank says that a restriction in their local file is not honoured, and the platform team wants a runbook step that explains why on their machine. Which two commands does the runbook name?

options.text: /memory, which shows the loaded files, and claude init, which writes a fresh settings file
options.says: Ruled out because a fresh settings file would hide the evidence, and the answer is "a lookup and not a guess".

options.text: /model, which shows the chosen model, and claude logout, which clears the stored session
options.says: Ruled out because the usual reasons for a policy that "does nothing" are "it is in a file the key does not read, a higher level sets the same key, or a lock removed the lower entry on purpose", and neither a model choice nor a sign-out shows which applies.

options.text: /permissions, which lists the rules, and claude update, which fetches the newest policy
options.says: Ruled out because the answer is "a lookup and not a guess", and a command that fetches a policy does not say what was dropped.

options.text: /status, which shows the setting sources, and claude doctor, which lists what was dropped
options.says: The page gives the lookup: "`/status` shows the `Setting sources` line, which names the managed source Claude Code selected, and `claude doctor` lists what it dropped" (module 92, page 1).

origin.section: Finding out what a machine is running

questions.stem: Scenario: Hart Media's platform team writes a managed MCP allowlist entry that gives both a server name and its address, believing two keys make the entry stricter. What does the page say about such an entry?

options.text: It is invalid
options.says: The page states the shape: "Each entry has exactly one of `serverName`, `serverCommand` or `serverUrl`: an entry with two keys is invalid" (module 92, page 2).

options.text: It is valid, and a developer's own list may widen it
options.says: Ruled out because "only the managed `allowedMcpServers` list applies and a developer's own list cannot widen it".

options.text: It is valid for a deny list, and invalid for an allow list only
options.says: Ruled out because the rule is about the entry itself, and "A denied server wins over an allowed one" is a different rule about two lists.

options.text: It is valid, and the same server may also sit in the deny list
options.says: Ruled out because "the same server never appears in both lists", so a server on the allowed list cannot also be denied.

origin.section: Where plugins and servers may come from
